paragraphs: A polynomial threshold function classifies an input according to the sign of a polynomial. This paper studies how to learn these classifiers actively, choosing queries to reduce the information needed. The starting obstacle is strong: existing lower bounds rule out nontrivial active learning even for quadratic polynomials with a single input variable under traditional access.

The authors change what information the learner can request. With basic access to derivatives of the underlying classifier, they give a computationally efficient method for learning degree-d polynomials in one variable. Its query bound is roughly cubic in d and logarithmic in the inverse accuracy and confidence parameters, with additional logarithmic factors suppressed. They also extend the method to batches, trading query complexity against the number of adaptive rounds.

Further algorithms are near optimal in several average-case settings. However, the extra derivative information does not resolve the problem generally: the paper proves that it is insufficient for multivariate polynomial threshold functions, even with only two variables. The contribution therefore identifies both a useful information source and a sharp boundary on its power.
neurips-2022-active-learning-polynomial-.tldr: Derivative access enables efficient active learning of one-variable polynomial threshold functions, but remains insufficient even for two-variable ones.

paragraphs: A graph generator can produce examples without making its underlying probability model available in an explicit form. This makes assessing its output a distinct statistical problem. AgraSSt addresses that problem by asking whether a learned generation process can produce graphs resembling a given input graph, rather than requiring an explicit formula for the full generator.

The method constructs a kernel discrepancy using an operator obtained from the generator. Its design draws on Stein operators for random graphs, turning properties of the generating process into a statistical comparison. This provides a way to evaluate a generator through the relationship between its implied graph behavior and the graph being used as a reference.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for a broad class of random graph models and empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world graphs. Synthetic examples have known generation procedures, while the real-world examples are used to train advanced graph generators. AgraSSt can also provide interpretable criticism of training and help identify reliable sample batches, making assessment potentially useful for improving generators and selecting outputs for later tasks.
neurips-2022-agrasst-approximate-graph-s.tldr: AgraSSt uses a generator-derived statistical discrepancy to assess graph generators and provide interpretable feedback without requiring an explicit probability model.

paragraphs: This paper studies causal effect estimation when useful data are spread across multiple sources that cannot share their raw training records. The sources may follow different distributions, so combining information requires accounting for differences between them. The proposed federated framework aims to learn heterogeneous causal effects while adapting how information transfers across sources.

The method uses Random Fourier Features to separate the loss into components associated with individual data sources. It then learns transfer coefficients that express similarities among those sources. Consequently, the procedure does not require similarity measures to be specified beforehand. Causal effects are incorporated independently and systematically, allowing the framework to accommodate the disparate distributions represented in the decentralized data.

The authors also derive minimax lower bounds to assess the quality of parameters learned across sources. Experiments show improvements over the evaluated baselines when source distributions differ. Because raw training data remain with their respective sources, the approach reduces exposure associated with exchanging those records. The abstract presents this as minimizing privacy leakage risk, rather than as a formal differential privacy guarantee.
neurips-2022-an-adaptive-kernel-approach.tldr: An adaptive federated method learns how to transfer information across dissimilar data sources to estimate causal effects without exchanging raw training data.

paragraphs: Gaussian process approximations often handle large numbers of observations more successfully than large numbers of input features. As feature counts grow, maintaining predictive quality can require rapidly increasing the number of variables used to summarize the data. This paper addresses that second scaling problem while retaining efficient handling of many observations.

The authors introduce a kernel whose number of summarizing variables can grow exponentially with input dimension while computational cost grows only linearly in both observations and features. The key construction is called the Bezier buttress. It enables approximate inference without computing matrix inverses or determinants, providing the mechanism behind the claimed scaling rather than merely reducing the number of summarizing variables.

The paper also shows close similarities between the proposed kernel and several commonly used kernels for Gaussian process regression. Empirical results demonstrate scaling on datasets that are both tall, with many observations, and wide, with many features. The contribution is a kernel and inference construction that can support a rapidly expanding summary representation without paying a correspondingly exponential computational cost.
neurips-2022-bezier-gaussian-processes-f.tldr: Bezier Gaussian processes use a new kernel and inference construction to scale linearly with both observation count and input dimension.

paragraphs: A classifier can struggle when its test images come from a different distribution than its training images. Domain generalization tries to prepare for these unseen settings using the available source domains. This paper proposes addressing the problem by explicitly learning which image features are specific to each source domain and then removing those features.

The framework, called LRDG, assigns different roles to its components. First, a classifier learns domain-specific features for each source domain. An encoder-decoder network then transforms input images into a new image space where those learned features are removed. A separate classifier trains on the transformed images to learn features intended to remain useful across domains.

This design makes image transformation the bridge between identifying domain dependence and learning a more transferable classifier. The final classifier receives images processed to reduce the domain-specific information identified earlier. Extensive experiments report better performance than the state-of-the-art methods used for comparison. These findings support the proposed learn-and-remove strategy empirically; they do not establish that every transformed image is free of all possible domain-specific information.
neurips-2022-domain-generalization-by-le.tldr: LRDG learns domain-specific image features, removes them through an encoder-decoder, and trains a classifier on the resulting images to improve generalization.

paragraphs: Learning a 3D-aware image generator from 2D image collections becomes expensive at high resolution because of volumetric rendering. A common solution adds a 2D decoder that enlarges low-resolution outputs from a 3D generator. The paper identifies drawbacks of that design: shape and texture can change with the camera viewpoint, and learned geometry can have low fidelity.

EpiGRAF instead trains a pure 3D generator using image patches. The authors improve patch-based optimization with a discriminator that accounts for patch location and scale, allowing it to handle different spatial positions and proportions. They also introduce a patch sampling strategy based on an annealed beta distribution, intended to stabilize training and speed convergence.

The model is evaluated on four datasets, including two introduced in the work, at resolutions of 256 by 256 and 512 by 512. It achieves state-of-the-art image quality, high-fidelity geometry, and approximately 2.5 times faster training than the compared upsampler-based systems. The results show that patch-wise training can make high-resolution pure 3D generation practical without relying on a separate 2D enlargement stage.
neurips-2022-epigraf-rethinking-training.tldr: EpiGRAF improves patch-wise training to produce high-resolution pure 3D generators with strong image quality, detailed geometry, and faster training.

paragraphs: In multi-label classification, an example can carry several labels, and some of those labels may be wrong. A noise transition matrix describes how clean labels become noisy ones. Methods that use this matrix depend heavily on estimating it well, but existing estimators often require anchor points or accurate estimates of noisy class probabilities.

The paper first studies when a class-dependent transition matrix can be identified from multi-label data. It then builds an estimator around correlations between labels. The method estimates how often two noisy labels appear together and selects samples that reveal information about clean-label correlations. That information helps estimate how often a noisy label occurs when a particular clean label is present.

Differences between the correlations expressed by these occurrence probabilities provide the information used to identify the transition matrix. The matrix is recovered through a bilinear decomposition, without requiring anchor points or accurate fitting of the noisy class posterior. Empirical results show effective matrix estimation and improved classification. The central contribution is to make relationships among labels informative about label corruption, rather than estimating each label's noise in isolation.
neurips-2022-estimating-noise-transition.tldr: The paper estimates multi-label noise transition matrices from label correlations without requiring anchor points or accurately fitted noisy class probabilities.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes a deep linear network with weight decay and stochastic neurons. Although the network is linear, its layered parameterization provides a model for studying neural network optimization. The authors derive an analytical expression for its global minima, giving an exact description of the best solutions within the model they study.

The analysis highlights zero as a special point in the optimization landscape. Weight decay interacts strongly with network architecture and can create bad minima at zero when the network has more than one hidden layer. The behavior is qualitatively different from the case with a single hidden layer. Depth therefore changes how the regularization term influences optimization, even in this linear setting.

The practical implication concerns initialization: the results indicate that common initialization methods are insufficient to ease neural network optimization in general. This is not a claim that those methods always fail. Instead, the exact model exposes an architectural interaction with weight decay that initialization alone does not generally resolve, connecting an analytical landscape result to a familiar training choice.
neurips-2022-exact-solutions-of-a-deep-l.tldr: Exact analysis of a deep linear network shows that weight decay can create bad zero-valued minima when the network has multiple hidden layers.

paragraphs: Few-shot image classification often starts with a feature extractor trained on many base examples and adapts it to novel classes with very few examples. That adaptation can overfit because the novel dataset is so small. FeLMi addresses this shortage by generating synthetic training samples through manifold mixup, combining information within the learned feature representation.

The method distinguishes between possible mixed samples using an uncertainty-based criterion. It selects hard mixup samples instead of treating all synthetic combinations alike. FeLMi also mixes base and novel examples and uses entropy-based filtering to make better use of pseudo-labeled base examples. Together, these choices aim to provide more useful adaptation data from the examples already available.

Experiments cover FC-100, CIFAR-FS, miniImageNet, and tieredImageNet, with reported improvements in both one-shot and five-shot settings. The authors also report significant improvements when transferring from miniImageNet to CUB in a cross-domain few-shot setting. These results support the usefulness of selecting challenging mixtures and incorporating filtered base examples when adapting a feature extractor to classes with scarce labeled data.
neurips-2022-felmi-few-shot-learning-wit.tldr: FeLMi improves few-shot adaptation by selecting uncertain mixup samples and combining novel examples with filtered, pseudo-labeled base examples.

paragraphs: Dynamic linear regression allows the predictor vector to change over time. The paper models this as a linear dynamical system with a changing observation operator and studies how to estimate the variances of process noise and observation noise. Existing approaches lack either guarantees altogether or explicit rates describing accuracy with a finite amount of data.

The authors analyze the global system operator, which maps noise vectors to observed outputs. By estimating its spectrum, they connect variance estimation accuracy to the geometry of the system. Their bounds depend on the shape of a related spectrum, making explicit which data characteristics influence convergence rather than only asserting that estimation eventually succeeds.

This yields what the authors identify as the first variance estimators for the problem with finite-sample complexity guarantees. The results cover arbitrary sub-Gaussian noise distributions, rather than only a single noise distribution within that class. Evaluations use both synthetic and real-world benchmarks. The main contribution is a quantitative connection between the system's structure and estimation error when the available dataset is finite.
neurips-2022-finite-sample-analysis-of-d.tldr: The paper derives finite-sample guarantees for dynamic regression noise-variance estimation by linking estimation error to the spectrum of the system operator.

paragraphs: This paper considers sequential selection from candidates belonging to sensitive groups, where rewards may not be directly comparable across groups. Its fairness criterion selects the candidate with the highest relative standing within their own group. The motivation is that raw reward differences can reflect discrimination or social injustice rather than comparable merit.

Relative standing is not directly observed, so the algorithm must estimate both rewards and their group-specific distributions. The proposed greedy policy fits ridge regression to observed context-reward pairs and uses empirical cumulative distributions to estimate each candidate's rank. The analysis assumes that contexts are independent between groups and that each group's reward distribution is absolutely continuous.

Under these conditions, the policy achieves fair pseudo-regret of order square root of dT, up to logarithmic factors, with high probability, despite having no initial exploration phase. It also satisfies demographic parity each round when averaged over all possible prior information. Simulations and US census experiments show sublinear fair pseudo-regret in practice, supporting the possibility of learning this relative-rank criterion while making sequential decisions.
neurips-2022-group-meritocratic-fairness.tldr: A greedy contextual bandit policy learns to select candidates by within-group reward rank, with conditional fairness and regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Many 2D pose estimation systems predict heatmaps indicating where body joints are located. Training commonly replaces each annotated joint point with a Gaussian-smoothed heatmap and penalizes pixel-wise differences from that target. This paper shows that improving such a heatmap objective may not consistently improve the actual task: locating the body joint accurately.

The proposed method changes the training formulation to distribution matching. It compares the predicted heatmap directly with the joint's dot annotation, avoiding construction of a Gaussian-smoothed target. This changes what the optimization is asked to match, bringing the annotated location itself into the objective rather than measuring only pixel-level agreement with a manufactured heatmap.

The authors report that this formulation can produce more consistent improvements in joint localization as heatmap optimization proceeds. Experiments on COCO and MPII demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The significance is the distinction between success on a convenient intermediate training target and success on the underlying prediction task: a heatmap loss can improve without localization improving in step, motivating a more direct distribution-based objective.
neurips-2022-heatmap-distribution-matchi.tldr: Matching predicted heatmaps directly to joint-point annotations can align pose-estimation training more consistently with accurate joint localization.

paragraphs: Choosing a language-model architecture involves balancing perplexity against latency and peak memory on particular hardware. Lightweight Transformer Search builds on an empirical observation: decoder parameter count strongly correlates with the ranking of autoregressive Transformer performance across architecture topologies. It uses that count as a proxy for perplexity, eliminating model training during architecture search.

The search measures hardware costs directly on target devices and identifies a Pareto frontier of quality-cost trade-offs using its proxy. It does not require GPUs for the search itself. Evaluations span ARM CPUs and NVIDIA GPUs, using GPT-2 and Transformer-XL, so the hardware measurements inform architecture selection for different deployment settings.

Compared with the respective 16-layer models, selected architectures match perplexity with up to 1.5 and 2.5 times faster runtime and 1.2 and 2.0 times lower peak memory. In zero- and one-shot evaluations across 14 tasks, frontier models exceed the average accuracy of 350M-parameter OPT with up to 1.6 times lower latency. Search finishes in under three hours on a commodity laptop. These are empirical results based on a performance proxy, not a guarantee that parameter count perfectly predicts every architecture's quality.
neurips-2022-litetransformersearch-train.tldr: LTS searches for efficient Transformer architectures without training candidates, using decoder parameter count as a performance proxy and measuring hardware costs directly.

paragraphs: In incremental semantic segmentation, a model learns new classes over successive training stages. Forgetting becomes particularly difficult when the meaning of background changes: objects learned previously can be labeled as background in the current stage. Training on those labels can weaken the model's knowledge of old concepts even though the corresponding objects remain visible.

MicroSeg starts from the assumption that background regions with strong objectness may represent concepts from earlier or future stages. A proposal generator first divides an image into hundreds of candidate segments. Background proposals with strong objectness are then clustered and assigned newly defined labels during optimization, giving these regions a more differentiated training role.

The intention is to preserve information about how old concepts are distributed in feature space, reducing forgetting caused by changing background semantics. The assumption is deliberately about possible membership in other-stage concepts, not certainty that every object-like region belongs to an old class. Competitive results on Pascal VOC and ADE20K support the effectiveness of this strategy for incremental segmentation.
neurips-2022-mining-unseen-classes-via-r.tldr: MicroSeg clusters object-like background regions into additional labels to reduce forgetting caused by shifting background meanings in incremental segmentation.

paragraphs: Random exploration during reinforcement learning can produce dangerous behavior before an agent learns a useful policy. This paper works within constrained Markov decision processes, where transitions produce costs as well as rewards. The objective is to maximize accumulated reward while keeping accumulated cost below a prescribed threshold during training and deployment.

The proposed on-policy algorithm learns an environment transition model online and combines it with a constrained version of proximal policy optimization using Lagrangian relaxation. An ensemble of neural networks with different initializations addresses uncertainty in environment modeling, including uncertainty associated with limited knowledge and variability in outcomes. The learned model and policy optimization jointly support the search for a feasible, rewarding policy.

Evaluation takes place in OpenAI Safety Gym against constrained model-free and model-based approaches. The method uses samples more efficiently and accumulates fewer hazard violations than the compared constrained model-free methods. It also achieves better rewards than the compared constrained model-based methods. These reported improvements support safer and more efficient learning in the benchmark; the stated empirical result is reduced violations, not elimination of all unsafe behavior.
neurips-2022-model-based-safe-deep-reinf.tldr: An online environment model paired with constrained PPO improves sample efficiency and reduces hazard violations in the reported safe reinforcement learning evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper establishes limits on statistical estimation under approximate differential privacy, expressed through epsilon and delta. A lower bound specifies how many samples a private method must have to achieve the relevant estimation objective. Such results help distinguish shortcomings of particular algorithms from sample requirements imposed by privacy and the statistical problem itself.

For Gaussian covariance estimation, the authors prove dimension-dependent lower bounds of order d squared under Frobenius-norm error and d to the three-halves under spectral-norm error. These match upper bounds up to logarithmic factors. The main technical contribution is a broad extension of the fingerprinting method to exponential families, which supplies the tool for proving these covariance bounds.

The paper also uses a private Assouad method to prove a tight lower bound of order d divided by alpha squared times epsilon for mean estimation with bounded covariance and alpha error in Euclidean distance. Earlier lower bounds were polynomially weaker or required pure differential privacy. The results therefore sharpen known sample requirements while covering the less restrictive approximate-privacy setting.
neurips-2022-new-lower-bounds-for-privat.tldr: The paper proves tight or nearly tight sample lower bounds for private covariance and mean estimation using an expanded fingerprinting technique.

paragraphs: Stochastic preprocessing defenses randomly transform inputs before a model makes predictions. A common rationale is that this randomness makes adversarial inputs harder to construct. The paper examines that belief theoretically and empirically, asking whether random preprocessing actually disrupts attacks enough to provide the protection often attributed to it.

The authors find that most stochastic defenses have insufficient randomness to withstand even standard projected gradient descent attacks. This challenges the assumption that attackers must explicitly average over transformations through Expectation over Transformation whenever a defense is stochastic. In the studied defenses, randomness alone often does not make conventional attack procedures ineffective.

The analysis also identifies a trade-off involving model invariance. As a model becomes less sensitive to the defense's random transformations, those transformations become less effective as a defense. Thus, the relevant question is not merely whether an input is randomized, but how that randomization interacts with the model's response. The authors argue that future approaches need to decouple robustness from this invariance effect, rather than treating inference-time randomness as sufficient protection.
neurips-2022-on-the-limitations-of-stoch.tldr: Most studied stochastic preprocessing defenses remain vulnerable to standard attacks, and their effectiveness declines as models become invariant to their randomization.

paragraphs: Imitation learning seeks a policy using expert behavior as guidance. This paper studies the infinite-horizon setting with linear function approximation and develops algorithms with rigorous efficiency guarantees without restrictive coherence assumptions. It starts from a minimax formulation and uses classical optimization tools to simplify how the learning problem is solved.

For online imitation learning, the proximal-point method replaces conventional alternating policy evaluation and cost updates. Instead, the algorithm optimizes one smooth convex objective jointly over cost and Q-functions. The analysis also addresses approximate optimization: when the objective is not solved exactly, it relates the remaining optimization error to the suboptimality of the recovered policy.

A second interpretation views the proximal-point construction as dual smoothing centered on the expert policy. This yields an offline algorithm with guarantees on the required number of expert trajectories. Experiments report strong performance with both linear and neural network function approximation. The theoretical efficiency setting is linear approximation, while the empirical work additionally demonstrates the approach with neural networks.
neurips-2022-proximal-point-imitation-le.tldr: Proximal-point optimization and dual smoothing yield simpler online and offline imitation-learning algorithms with guarantees under linear function approximation.

paragraphs: Sharpness-Aware Minimization aims to find network weights in relatively flat regions of the loss landscape. It does this through a minimax objective that considers the largest nearby loss as well as the loss at the current weights. In practice, the inner maximization is commonly approximated with one gradient-ascent step to keep training manageable.

The paper focuses on the quality of that approximation. One ascent step may be insufficient, while taking multiple steps increases training cost. The proposed Random Sharpness-Aware Minimization method uses random smoothing to smooth the loss landscape. It then applies a single ascent step on the smoothed weights to improve the approximation of the inner maximization.

The authors evaluate R-SAM on CIFAR and ImageNet with ResNets and Vision Transformers, reporting consistent performance improvements in those experiments. The approach therefore targets how the sharpness objective is approximated, using smoothing to improve the usefulness of a one-step update. The reported evidence supports the method across the tested datasets and architecture families, rather than establishing that smoothing improves every possible training setup.
neurips-2022-random-sharpness-aware-mini.tldr: R-SAM smooths the loss landscape to improve SAM's one-step inner maximization and reports better ResNet and Vision Transformer performance.

paragraphs: Backpropagation determines how individual neural network connections should change to reduce an error. Whether the brain can perform a comparable form of credit assignment remains unclear. Earlier biologically motivated models either struggle to send error information through many layers or require separate learning phases. BurstCCN proposes a cortical network model that addresses both issues.

The model combines bursting activity, short-term plasticity, and interneurons that target dendrites. Connection-specific short-term plasticity enables burst multiplexing, allowing backpropagation-like error signals to travel through the network. Those signals are encoded at distal dendrites, where excitatory and inhibitory inputs from higher levels produce burst-dependent changes in connections.

The authors demonstrate error propagation across multiple layers within a single learning phase. Analytical and empirical results show that the resulting updates approximate backpropagation-derived gradients, and the model learns MNIST and CIFAR-10 image classification tasks. These findings suggest that cortical mechanisms operating at several biological scales could jointly support efficient deep learning. They establish the capabilities of the proposed model, rather than demonstrating that the brain necessarily uses this exact learning procedure.
neurips-2022-single-phase-deep-learning-.tldr: BurstCCN combines cortical mechanisms to propagate backpropagation-like errors through deep networks in one learning phase.

paragraphs: Few-shot classifiers can make predictions by comparing an input's embedding with embeddings representing class prototypes. This differs from directly producing class probabilities. Existing randomized smoothing defenses rely heavily on the latter structure, leaving a gap for models whose decisions are based on distances in a learned representation space.

The paper extends randomized smoothing to few-shot models that produce normalized embeddings. Its analysis studies Lipschitz continuity, which describes how strongly a model's output can change as its input changes. The authors use this analysis to derive a robustness certificate for adversarial perturbations bounded in Euclidean, or l2, norm, bringing provable protection into the embedding-based setting.

Experiments on multiple datasets confirm the theoretical results. The significance is that robustness analysis can be adapted to the representation used for prototype comparisons, rather than depending only on class-probability outputs. The certificate concerns the stated normalized-embedding models and bounded perturbations. The authors describe its usefulness for few-shot scenarios as a possibility supported by the theory and experiments, rather than a guarantee covering every few-shot learning method.
neurips-2022-smoothed-embeddings-for-cer.tldr: The paper extends randomized smoothing to normalized embeddings and derives l2 robustness certificates relevant to prototype-based few-shot learning.

paragraphs: Molecular conformer generation seeks different three-dimensional configurations of a molecule. This paper proposes a diffusion framework that works in the space of torsion angles. The choice makes rotational degrees of freedom central to generation, with a diffusion process defined on a hypertorus, the mathematical space used here to represent multiple periodic angles together.

The framework combines that process with an extrinsic-to-intrinsic score model. Its design connects the score model to the angular space where diffusion operates. On a standard benchmark of drug-like molecules, the generated conformer ensembles outperform the compared machine learning and cheminformatics approaches in both RMSD and chemical properties. The method is also orders of magnitude faster than previous diffusion-based models.

A further capability is exact likelihood calculation. The authors use it to construct what they describe as the first generalizable Boltzmann generator. Thus, the contribution extends beyond producing geometrically strong conformers: the model also supplies probability information that supports another molecular generation task. The performance claims concern the stated benchmark and comparisons, while the angular diffusion framework is the central methodological advance.
neurips-2022-torsional-diffusion-for-mol.tldr: Torsional diffusion generates strong molecular conformer ensembles efficiently by diffusing over torsion angles and also provides exact likelihoods.

paragraphs: A generated summary can read fluently while misrepresenting its source document. This paper identifies two possible contributors: the model may fail to capture the document's key information, or it may rely too heavily on language-model preferences when choosing words. Faithfulness Enhanced Summarization addresses these possibilities through separate but connected training mechanisms.

First, question answering tests whether the encoder captures information needed to answer questions about the document's central content. Attention from this task also guides where the summary decoder should attend in the source. Second, a max-margin loss based on the difference between the language model and summarization model aims to prevent excessive confidence from the language model.

These components connect summary generation more closely to source understanding and source-directed attention. Experiments on CNN/DM and XSum show significant improvements over strong baselines, while factual-consistency evaluation finds more faithful summaries. The results support the proposed combination as a way to reduce unfaithfulness; the two motivating causes are presented as possible explanations, not an exhaustive account of every factual error.
neurips-2022-towards-improving-faithfuln.tldr: FES combines question-answering guidance with a loss that discourages language-model overconfidence to generate more faithful summaries.

paragraphs: This paper argues that predicting the correct disease is only part of an acceptable automatic diagnosis system. During an initial interaction, the evidence may support several plausible diseases rather than a definitive answer. Doctors also investigate severe possibilities and need to understand how collected evidence supports the proposed diagnoses.

The authors formulate evidence acquisition and diagnosis using deep reinforcement learning. The framework incorporates three aspects of the reasoning process: maintaining a differential diagnosis, following an exploration-confirmation approach, and prioritizing severe pathologies. These choices make the sequence of patient interactions part of the learning objective, alongside the eventual disease prediction.

The paper introduces interaction-quality metrics reflecting those three aspects. Evaluation shows improvements over existing models while preserving competitive pathology prediction accuracy. The contribution is therefore a broader training and evaluation target: a system should gather evidence in a way that supports plausible alternatives and attends to serious conditions. The reported results support better measured interaction behavior, rather than establishing clinical trust or acceptance solely from prediction performance.
neurips-2022-towards-trustworthy-automat.tldr: A reinforcement learning diagnosis framework improves measured interaction quality by maintaining differential diagnoses, exploring and confirming evidence, and prioritizing severe diseases.

paragraphs: Invariant learning seeks features that remain reliable when aspects of the data distribution change. Many methods rely on data already divided into environments, making those changes visible to the learner. This paper asks whether useful invariances can instead be learned when the data are heterogeneous but no environment partition is supplied.

The first result establishes an obstacle: without further inductive biases or additional information, identifying invariant features in this setting is fundamentally impossible. The proposed ZIN framework therefore uses auxiliary information to learn an environment partition and an invariant representation jointly. The extra information plays an explicit role in making identification possible, rather than leaving its contribution implicit.

The authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions for their framework to identify invariant features under a fairly general setting. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the analysis and demonstrate improved performance. The work contributes both a method and an explanation of what enables it: learning invariance without predefined environments requires some additional basis for distinguishing stable structure from variation in the observed data.
neurips-2022-zin-when-and-how-to-learn-i.tldr: ZIN uses auxiliary information to jointly learn environments and invariant features, after showing that the task is impossible without additional information or inductive biases.
